analysis.one_liner: Protects abortion access nationwide by striking state restrictions that clinics and providers call unnecessary.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill: it was referred to the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced in May 2019 and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would bar state and local governments from imposing a long list of abortion-specific restrictions: medically unnecessary tests and in-person visits, requirements that one provider perform all related care, mandates that doctors read state-scripted information, hospital transfer agreements and building rules not applied to similar procedures, and bans on abortion before fetal viability or after viability when the patient's health is at risk. It would strike down restrictions already on the books, and let the Justice Department, patients, and providers sue to block ones that follow. States defending a restriction would have to prove, with clear and convincing evidence, that it significantly advances patient safety and that no less restrictive option exists.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients seeking abortion care, especially low-income women, women of color, young people, immigrants, and people in rural or underserved areas, who under the bill's own findings bear the heaviest burden of traveling long distances and making multiple visits. Abortion clinics and providers also gain, because rules that apply only to them — building codes, hospital privilege requirements, physician-only laws — could no longer be enforced.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Abortion patients, especially low-income and rural women

how_it_helps.text: Bars state rules requiring medically unnecessary tests and procedures, medically inaccurate counseling scripts, and mandatory extra in-person visits before an abortion.

Prohibits restrictions on clinic buildings, staffing, hospital transfer agreements, and provider hospital privileges that are not imposed on facilities performing medically comparable procedures, the kind of rules that have closed clinics.
Prohibits states from banning abortion before fetal viability, or after viability when the provider judges the pregnancy risks the patient's life or health.

Lets the Attorney General, individual patients, and health care providers sue for injunctions, and requires a state defending a restriction to prove by clear and convincing evidence that it significantly advances patient safety and cannot be replaced by a less restrictive measure.
Takes effect immediately and applies to restrictions enacted before it, so existing state rules conflicting with the Act could no longer be enforced.
Extends protection to all pregnant people regardless of sex, race, immigration status, age, or disability.

analysis.who_pays: State governments would lose the power to enact or enforce abortion restrictions, including ones already on their books. The bill creates no new federal spending; its costs to states come in the form of surrendered regulatory authority and the expense of defending lawsuits.

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts all conflicting state law — and federal law including the Religious Freedom Restoration Act — and applies retroactively, a sweeping federal override of rules that state legislatures enacted, including regulations that some voters support.

It prohibits bans on abortion before fetal viability and sets a demanding 'clear and convincing evidence' standard that a state must meet to keep any abortion-specific rule, which critics argue removes democratic decisions about abortion from the states entirely.
The bill does not touch insurance coverage of abortion, so coverage restrictions and cost barriers that fall hardest on low-income patients would remain in place even if the bill passed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients facing closed clinics, mandatory waiting trips, and bans, the protections would be substantial and directly practical. The real cost is one of principle rather than money: the bill deliberately strips states of abortion policymaking and overturns existing laws, which supporters see as necessary to end a patchwork of restrictions and opponents see as an overreach of federal power over matters many states have decided differently.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and the Senate never voted before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Richard Blumenthal introduced the bill on May 23, 2019 with 43 cosponsors — 41 Democrats and 2 independents — and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary that same day.
The action history shows no activity after the referral to Judiciary: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 without the Senate ever voting on the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State governments that restrict abortion and the advocacy movements behind those restrictions are better off, because the bill died without a vote and left their existing laws and authority untouched. Patients and providers in restrictive states were left with the access limits the bill was written to remove.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States keeping the power to restrict abortion

for.name: Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 43 Senate cosponsors.

for.name: 43 Senate Democratic and independent cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors at introduction; no Republican did.

against.name: Lindsey Graham
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred to his committee.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote in the roughly 19 months after its introduction.

against.name: Anti-abortion advocacy organizations
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal codification of abortion rights and lobbied Republican senators against such bills.

sides.party_line_note: All 43 cosponsors were Democrats or independents and none was a Republican; since no vote was ever held, the partisan split can be measured only by sponsorship, not by roll call.

industries.note: The bill guarantees providers a statutory right to perform abortions free of abortion-specific state rules, and gives them a new tool to sue. Their financial interest in staying open runs directly alongside patients' interest in nearby access.

States would lose authority to restrict abortion, including laws already enacted, and could be sued. The restrictions they have favored limit what patients can obtain, so their interest in this bill ran against patient access.

Rules that required clinics to maintain hospital transfer agreements and doctors to hold hospital privileges could no longer be enforced, easing pressure that pushed care into hospital settings. The bill does not otherwise change how hospitals are regulated.
